case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Kenosha County DHS v. Jodie W.
key_cases.holding: Terminating an incarcerated parent's rights under the continuing-CHIPS ground because she failed to meet a condition of return she could not possibly satisfy while imprisoned, without regard to her actual parenting or the child's condition, violates substantive due process.
key_cases.relevance: Court-ordered conditions of return must be ones the particular parent can actually meet; impossible conditions cannot support later unfitness.
key_cases.quote: the circuit court improperly deemed Jodie unfit solely by virtue of her status as an incarcerated person without regard for her actual parenting activities or the condition of her child

key_cases.case_name: Sheboygan County DHHS v. Tanya M.B.
key_cases.holding: A CHIPS dispositional order satisfies Wis. Stat. sec. 48.355(2)(b)1. without itemizing every service so long as it orders supervision, services and case management and sets detailed conditions; whether the agency made a 'reasonable effort' to provide those services is judged in light of the parents' cooperation.
key_cases.relevance: It is the controlling Wisconsin authority on what a court-ordered service plan must contain and how 'reasonable effort' is proved.
key_cases.quote: A relevant consideration in determining "reasonable effort" to provide services is the parents' "level of cooperation."

key_cases.case_name: Sallie T. v. Milwaukee County DHHS
key_cases.holding: A biological parent's compliance with the return-home conditions of a CHIPS dispositional order creates no presumption that returning the child is in the child's best interests; revision or extension remains a discretionary best-interests decision.
key_cases.relevance: It defines the legal weight of compliance with a court-ordered service plan.
key_cases.quote: We determine that compliance with a dispositional order is not dispositive of a child's best interests.

key_cases.holding: A juvenile court loses competency to act when a CHIPS dispositional order expires without a timely extension hearing beyond the single 30-day continuance, and no party can waive that loss of competency.
key_cases.relevance: Court-ordered supervision ends by operation of law if the extension deadline passes, regardless of the parties' acquiescence.
key_cases.quote: we hold that a party cannot waive the right to object to a court's loss of competence once the 30-day extension has passed without a hearing

key_cases.case_name: Eau Claire County DHS v. S.E.
key_cases.holding: TPR warning notice under Wis. Stat. sec. 48.356 must identify the grounds, including sub-parts, applicable when the CHIPS order is entered; a later amendment shortening the continuing-CHIPS timeframe did not require new notice and did not violate due process.
key_cases.relevance: Every court order continuing out-of-home placement must carry written warning of the TPR grounds then applicable.
key_cases.quote: Sophie's notice needed to identify only the grounds for termination that existed at the time of the initial CHIPS order.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act's requirement that a state make 'reasonable efforts' to prevent removal and to reunify families confers no privately enforceable right on children or families and creates no implied cause of action.
key_cases.relevance: The federal reasonable-efforts requirement behind Wisconsin's court-ordered service plans cannot itself be enforced by the family in federal court.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that 42 U. S. C. § 671 (a)(15) neither confers an enforceable private right on its beneficiaries nor creates an implied cause of action on their behalf.
